utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it was Mr. Pantelic's turn to respond, unless Mr. Di Fazio is speaking on the same point. Do you want to make some additional points on behalf of the Prosecution. Mr. Pantelic can reply later. MR. Di FAZIO: I do want to raise some additional matters on the issue that was raised yesterday afternoon. And my colleague Ms. Reidy has also prepared some further detailed submissions on the issue, and I had hoped that we would both be permitted to address the Chamber, provide you with a bit more information about the issue of the document that was provided to the Defence yesterday. And also to make some more submissions. I'll be brief because the bulk of the submission will be handled by Ms. Reidy, and I want to take this opportunity to underscore and emphasise the seriousness of the allegations that were made against the Prosecution yesterday. And to reiterate that this is not the first time that this sort of allegation has been made. Yesterday, the Prosecution was accused, and I am referring to the transcript now, of gross and blatant violations of the trial. Reference was made to the intolerable practice of the Prosecution in failing to provide documents it is obliged to provide, reference to a possible miscarriage of justice in this case, and there was a call made to you to impose sanctions to stop this practice. They are matters in my submission that go to the very heart of the proper conduct of this case and matters that go to the very heart of the conduct of the Prosecution in particular. The allegation is of gross and blatant violations, and secondly that this is part of a practice. This is not the first time that these very serious allegations have been made. Your Honours will recall recently the issue arose in the case of notes that I provided to the Defence regarding issues that Mr. Todorovic had spoken about, proofing notes in effect. And again, the same sort of language was used on that occasion, and again the same accusations were made. And in the reply, I submit, on that indication the Prosecution pointed out how innocuous and innocent the whole occasion had been and how when one looked at what had actually been provided to the Defence, the oversight of the Prosecution on that indication had left to nothing of any particular consequence. The Prosecution submission on this occasion will be, and my colleague Ms. Reidy will develop that, that again on this occasion it would have been desirable of course to provide the statement that was provided yesterday, but that again, no miscarriage of justice has occurred, no potential miscarriage of justice has occurred. I rather expected as I began reading the transcript that I would not be met with any articulation of an actual miscarriage of justice from Mr. Pantelic. And indeed, if you look at the transcript, the allegations are made, and then he sits down. It's glaring on this occasion, and on the previous occasion, that he fails to develop any sort of argument articulating what the prejudice has been to the Defence, and that is something that my colleague Ms. Reidy will address you upon. I invite you to, of course, deal with this issue as you will in the firmest and clearest of terms. I reiterate that the Prosecution has made its best endeavours, and my colleague Ms. Reidy will give you a history of how we came to -- how this document came to light. Has used its best endeavours to provide these sorts of documents to the Defence as soon as they are uncovered, and that we have done and performed these sorts of efforts in the past. So I reject emphatically that there is a practice, that there has ever been any practice, of withholding documents from the Defence, and I reject and submit that it's completely incorrect to say that there has been a gross and blatant violation of the trial by the failure to hand over this particular document to the Defence yesterday. In my submission, the Trial Chamber should give the matter very serious consideration, considering the language used when these accusations are made against the Prosecution. I'd like to turn over the microphone to my colleague. She will provide you with a history of how this document was located, the possible uses that the Defence might have been able to make of this document, and that of course is connected with the question of was there any miscarriage of justice, was there any prejudice, was there any inconvenience caused to the Defence. And I would ask her to carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy. As briefly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to be brief, and I will as my colleague indicated try to focus on some practical matters about the disclosure of this document, which given the time we were not in a position to address yesterday. The first thing I would like to do also on a factual matter is to make a clarification, and an apology to the Bench for a statement I put on the record yesterday which upon rereading is probably not an accurate reflection of a statement. And I had stated yesterday that the statement disclosed, that of Sabrija Dagovic, did not mention the names of his sons in the statement. And I would like to correct that. Because the statement does mention the names of Safet and Esad, but does not directly indicate that those two persons that he refers to are his sons. And it was that consequence -- it was a consequence of that that I was referring to yesterday. And the consequences of that is that first when you initially read his statement, he talks about his sons, and then about two other people, and again on first blush reading it wasn't evident which is what I was trying to say yesterday. And secondly, the technical consequence of that is that when we do searches for witnesses, for example, Mr. Esad Dagovic, or Mr. Safet Dagovic, we would put in a criteria, for example, the name Esad within 50 words of Dagovic and hopefully bring up any document that possibly refers to him in it. This would not have been caught in any search like that. And that is why in that sense, his name specifically was not mentioned, nor specifically as being his son. So in the way I talked off the cuff yesterday; it may have been misleading, and I would like to apologise to my colleagues and to the Chamber if that was inaccurate. So I hope that I have clarified that. So to turn to the matter of the late disclosure of a document, and the impact it might have, I'd like to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention exactly what the nature of the document is, so that you can make a full assessment. It is a signed statement in total five pages, but of those five pages, only two and a half are actually a record of what the witness had said. The witness talks a lot about what happened in Bosanski Samac, the takeover, what happened to non-Serbs, how they weren't allowed to gather, how they had to wear armbands, how his son was arrested, how he had to go through forced labour. Basically he talks about all the crimes that happened in Bosanski Samac. However, in that statement, the only defendant he mentioned by name is Mr. Tadic, and he simply says that he was in charge of his exchange. No other defendant is mentioned in the statement. The controversial line of the document is the one where the defendants -- sorry, the witness says: "My sons were with a group of men who offered resistance throughout the first day. Both of my sons had weapons, and they participated in the fighting in the town. They came back home on Saturday morning about 9.30 on the 18th of April, 1992." And that is the only sentence in the whole statement which does not refer to crimes committed and things suffered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And are the sons being discussed in that quoted paragraph, actually, Esad and Safet?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: If you read on to the end and you begin to analyse the rest of his statement, you assume there's -- it's not clear, but you can make the assumption that it's Esad and Safet. It's not evident from it. That's the assumption we make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This particular maker of this statement, how many sons is he recorded to have?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I can check the statement. I think he just refers to his sons, not necessarily -- I'm not -- sorry, I did not have the statement in front of me. Here it is. Sorry. He doesn't say -- he says his family. I lived together with my family. So at no stage does he say it is limited to sons. I am working on the assumption that it is Esad and Safet that he is talking about and he doesn't have any others. But he certainly in his statement says, "I lived together with my family." He doesn't say anything whether he had daughters, how many sons, how many children, and that is the first mention he talks about his sons being away, and then much, much later in his statement, he refers to the fact that Esad was called on the phone by some 19 Chetniks who wanted him to give them 1.000 deutschmarks for [redacted] who was imprisoned in a camp. And I believe [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That is the basis of why this whole thing was initially disclosed to the Defence. Now, under Rule 68 we are obliged to disclose information which may suggest the innocence and mitigate the guilt that he's -- and this statement clearly does none of that. We are also obliged to disclose such things which may affect the credibility of the Prosecution evidence. And to the extent that this contradicts the position, if it does indeed, if that is Esad and Safet he's talking about, of what Mr. Dagovic has said on the stand, well, in that light it could be Rule 68, and that is why we disclosed it. Now, what is the impact of disclosing that yesterday? We would like to point out that the allegation which is in that statement, and giving a generous interpretation of that statement, that Esad Dagovic was out participating in the resistance on the night of the 16th and 17th is information which the Defence had for a long time in their possession and indeed has put on the record whilst Mr. Esad Dagovic was here on the stand. And I would draw the Chamber's attention to Prosecution Exhibit D29/3 where the statement which was put to the witness specifically refers to the allegations. And he says: "In response to questions of whether I had a firearm and whether I was in town with other individuals in order to prevent the disarming of citizens in Bosanski Samac, I state that this is not true because I did not have a firearm. All I had was a 9 millimetre zastava pistol for which I had a valid permit but which I handed over to the people who were disarming citizens in Bosanski Samac." So the substance of the allegation that is in his father's statement was already in the hands of the Defence, was put in this document to the defendant, and as I said, was on the record. So there is nothing new or revealing in the father's statement. I would also point out that this was put into evidence by the first Defence counsel to cross-examine the witness. So that Defence counsel and each Defence counsel who came after had the chance to follow up on this line of questioning if they so wanted. So the only prejudice, if that's what you want to call it, flowing from the late disclosure of that statement yesterday was the fact that they could not put to the witness that his father is recorded as having said that his sons were resisting. This Trial Chamber has consistently held that a statement of a third party cannot be put to a witness for his speculative comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think I may as well correct you there. That's not the point we are looking at here. It's the ability of the Defence to prepare their Defence properly having that type of information. I'm sure you appreciate that the impact is somewhat different when a statement is made by a father of one of the witnesses. Only crucial issue, was he participated in the conflict or not? Because from the cross-examination of some of the Prosecution witnesses, that is a point they are trying to make, that some of the people who were actually arrested and detained, whether rightly or wrongly, were actually arrested during the [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And my point would be they had information of the allegations that they had been participating already. The information they had to prepare their cross-examination. Could they have used this statement in the cross-examination? They couldn't have put a third party's statement to the witness for his comment. They could only have prepared the examination, put to him the allegation that you are participating in and what do you say about that? And they had the opportunity to do that from the information they already had. I'm just trying to assess to the extent to which any way they were prejudiced. Now that the Defence, as you said -- to help them prepare the Defence, the Defence now do have that statement. They know what the father said. It is now open to them. They are quite a number of months away from their Defence case. They are able to call in their Defence who they want. He is not a Prosecution witness. With that particular statement, there is nothing further on the cross-examination beyond putting the allegation to that witness they could have done, and of course they will have that opportunity to do that to his brother when he testifies after this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think it's right for you to lead me to that. The only way they could have used the statement was actually putting it to the Prosecution witnesses. They could have used it also to look for witnesses to support their Defence case. That is another possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, they are not excluded from doing that Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The point is because it has come to them at a late stage. You see the point I am making.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. At the end I also say that of course Mr. Dagovic could be recalled and could be recalled as part of the Defence case. If they put forward a case for that with good reason, I don't see why the Prosecution would oppose that. I would also in that sense like to address the fact that -- what I said is the trying to assess how just prejudicial the late disclosure of the document could be and whether or not this amounts to the very, very serious allegations of a miscarriage of justice, of gross and blatant violations of fairness of trial and of intolerable practices. And my colleagues have already noticed that these are allegations of the most grave kind, and we feel that Mr. Pantelic should be in a position to substantiate clearly these sort of allegations if he is going to put them on a public record. And this Tribunal has consistently held that matters of disclosure under Rule 68 that the burden is on the Defence who raised the matter to convince the Trial Chamber of Rule 68 material and how serious violations are that occurred. And in this case, Mr. Pantelic is calling in to question the good faith and integrity of the Prosecution in the way that they conducted their obligations. And in doing so, he has not provided one concrete example of how this fair trial has been jeopardised or irreparable has been caused. We would first on this matter note that the Prosecution's obligations under Rule 68 are also a matter of the Prosecutor's initial discretion as to whether something falls under Rule 68 or not. And in the Blaskic case, the Appeals Chamber had made clear that the initial decision as to whether evidence exculpatory has to be made to the Prosecutor without further proof that the Prosecution abused its judgement, that the Appeals Chamber would not interfere. So it was very clear that this discretion should be exercised in good faith and not abused. And in this case, the determination of whether or not a document falls under Rule 68 has always been done in good faith. What has occurred in this case is that two different witnesses have said contradictory things about an issue not relating to the defendants' conduct but to another matter. And on reading of first blush at an early stage in the trial, it is not unreasonable for a member of the Prosecutor's office to not deem it as a Rule 68 material. However, in exercising our diligence, using the opportunity given to us in this trial because of the unfortunate indisposition of his Honour Judge Singh we reviewed every single statement that has ever been taken from anybody to do with this case in light of the evidence that we now as the Prosecution team have heard, and in reading that for the first time and knowing Mr. Dagovic's testimony as we have heard on the stand, we could see that sentence put in that context as now giving rise to a Rule 68 obligation, and we so disclosed. Again, we would submit that that is not an abuse of our discretion, nor is it showing lack of good faith. The Blaskic Chamber has also pointed out that this discretion under Rule 68 is in part and of necessity tinged with subjectivity. And we would say it is no more evident than when we were dealing with this sort of issue, as I said an issue between two different witnesses saying contradictory things about an issue which does not go to the act or conduct of one of the accused. And I would also note, as the Trial Chamber did, that the possibility is always reserved to this Trial Chamber to verify on a case by case basis where there has been potential failures, to draw the necessary exclusions as to the probative value to be given to evidence in question. In the Blaskic case where the Defence tried to seek sanctions for what they alleged was continuing violations of Rule 68 which was rejected by both the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber, the Trial Chamber noted that Rule 68 is governed less by system of sanctions than by the Judges' definitive evaluation of the evidence presented by either of the parties and the possibility which the opposing party will have had to contest it. And in this case, we would submit it is clear the Defence have not been deprived of any ability to test the evidence. And they still have the opportunity to argue the probative value of all of this before the Chamber. So to sum up the Prosecution's position is one that the statement has now been disclosed and the Defence are in a position to prepare the Defence with the use of the statement. Any prejudice caused by the delay, we would submit, is minimal, but is also not irreparable. Safet Dagovic has yet to testify, and Esa Dagovic could be recalled, and as we said, was subject to cross-examination, and of course Masbia Dagovic has also been brought to the attention of the Defence. We also submit that while we are open always to errors, we have never acted in anything but good faith and we have never abused our discretion under Rule 68. Mr. Pantelic, as we have said, has made the most serious of allegations which he has never to date substantiated. He has talked of warnings given by the Trial Chamber and I can find no warning. We are aware of our obligations under Rule 68 and other disclosure provisions, and we will continue to review all the evidence for a fourth and for a fifth time with a new set of eyes and a new perspective and of being overconsciousness in our re-evaluation of what may or may not be Rule 68 brings us into a miscarriage of justice yet we would submit that that is not necessarily a just interpretation of Rule 68. And on the contrary, the Prosecution position is that the Chamber should consider whether Mr. Pantelic should be reprimanded by the Chamber for repeatedly making the most grave and serious allegations if he is not in a position to provide concrete substantiation for calling into question on the public record the integrity and good faith of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. First of all, allow me to thank to my learned friends from the Prosecution for the apologies made with regard to the issue raised yesterday by Ms. Reidy with regard to the mention with the names of the sons of witness Sabrija Dagovic, the statement from 1995. And I think this practice should be present here from the part of the Prosecution. From time to time, it's better to think twice and then say something. It will save our precious time here. I would like, before my submission, to emphasise the words of our learned colleague, Mr. Weiner, from yesterday's hearing. It is page 7040, line 4 and 7, from 4 to 7. The issue was after the question of her Honour Judge Mumba with regard to the statement in question, and the response was: "Which is long before any of the three of our counsel have been here. We have continued to look through the records. If we find anything, we immediately turn it over to the Defence counsel which is our obligation. This is not the witness that is going to testify." Your Honours, it is totally unacceptable, as a matter of principle, to hear these kind of explanations, because my understanding of the institution of the Prosecution office is that - and this is a fact - they are number and number of experts there. Senior trial attorneys, team leaders, et cetera, et cetera. It will not be appropriate that in each case when the team of the Prosecution members will change, this kind of approach should be done, because this is an institution. It is not tolerable that each new team of the Prosecutor members will raise this issue and say, well, it was in the past with our former colleagues. We don't know anything. We are ongoing procedures, et cetera, et cetera. I will respectfully remind this Trial Chamber that the indictment was filed in 1995, which means almost seven years ago. It is absolutely enough time for the Prosecution to prepare its case and to bring its case and to be ready for the trial. And it's not tolerable practice that during the trial, this kind of explanation even should be raised here. Another point: On the same page, line 12 until 18, Mr. Weiner made a reference that the Prosecution is in possession of 2.5 million documents with regard to this case. According to our --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's totally untrue. And he knows it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is the correct version?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: 2.5 million documents we are in possession of. That's the whole Tribunal, all the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For all the cases. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Which don't have 2.5 million documents in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my point. Reading his words, he mentioned 2.5 million documents, which brings me to another problem. Officially I would like to respectfully move this Trial Chamber to give a ruling or order and to allow the Defence team to make an inspection of all 2.5 million documents in possession of the OTP with regard to this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You have heard the correction. It's the whole Prosecution office on all the cases. It's not only on Simic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. But still, Your Honour, this particular witness statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're going back to it. That's the one you should be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It obviously related to this particular case called Simic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is no doubt about that. So I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You should direct your response more to the prejudice, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's my intention, Your Honour. So the practice of handling of this witness statement related to Simic case is very simple. All witness statements of Simic case are in the Simic case, not within the 2.5 million documents in possession of the OTP. This is a simple and regular, I would say, approach how one will handle document pertaining to certain particular case. It is not a document of the other institution, or it is not the document related to another case. This document, Your Honours, is hundred per cent related to Simic case. And the question is here: How this document which was made in 1995 was given to the Defence in 2002? That's the point. With regard to the -- with regard to the issue which I raised yesterday, I'm glad to give precise and factual explanations about the -- about the manner how the Prosecution team in this case is acting. Your Honours, allow me to first draw your attention to the issue of Prosecution and NATO SFOR forces in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic we haven't got all day. We are dealing with that particular document. I directed you to inform the Trial Chamber, point out how the late disclosure is affecting your client's case or the Defence case, what prejudice if any. I want you to restrict your submissions to that. Because if late disclosure does not occasion any prejudice, then we go ahead with the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I want to establish my grounds, because my learned friends asked me to give particular proofs, and I am going to give these proofs. So first of all, I can check in the transcript with regard to the confidential agreement between Prosecution and NATO why this agreement was not disclosed to the Defence. And furthermore, on the pretrial conference held on June 26th last year, on the page 876, line 18, Mr. Di Fazio said: "Firstly, I just want to state that as far as the Prosecution is concerned, disclosure has now been completed. This afternoon, we will provide about five further statements to the Defence. We have good reason for believing that that material has already been disclosed, but as -- from an abundance of the caution, we will hand it over again. To generally speaking disclosure of Rule 66 and 68 has been completed by the Prosecution." Then, Your Honour, on the -- here on the September 10th, page 915, line 7 and 12, we also discussed this matter, this obligation. On November the 2nd, last year, 2001, page 3306, we also raised this issue with regard to the practice of the discovery -- the disclosure from the side of the Prosecution. Then again, November 27, quite extensive discussion from page 4552 until 4568. Then on the 17th of January this year, 2002, there was also discussion with regard to this practice with a certain version of statements, et cetera. And also on the 18 of February, page 5987, the Defence raised this particular issue, which, Your Honours, bring us to the 19th of February this year and the ruling of this Trial Chamber with regard to the practice, and I will just interalia, page -- and page 6018, line 1 to 9, interalia I will just make the reference of the ruling of this Honourable Trial Chamber which said: "If at any stage the Trial Chamber finds that new details which are material to the Defence which have not been disclosed before, the Trial Chamber will take appropriate action, and this habit, if repeated by the Prosecution, may lead to undermining the Prosecution case altogether because it is likely to lead to an unfair trial to the accused." That was a ruling. Then, Your Honour, after that ruling, on the 1st of March, the Defence raised the same problem, page 6652. And that was a response of our friend, Mr. Di Fazio. First of all, the interview in July last year, Mr. Pantelic is correct that it was disclosed to the Defence late. I think it should -- I should take the fault for that. And then on the next page, 6653, he said: "It is a matter that I regret." Your Honours, very often here in these proceedings, we are listening of apologies of regrets, et cetera, from the part of the Prosecution. I think it is not enough to ensure the fairness of trial. I can elaborate, but I think it is not a proper moment now, because this is a part of Defence strategy, how and when we shall use certain statements, portion of statements, or documents, in our Defence case. That will be in our case. Now, we don't want to speculate how and when and to which extent certain portion of the late disclosure will affect our case. For the illustration, theoretically, speaking about this particular statement from 1995, which was disclosed yesterday, theoretically, the Defence would be in a situation if the Defence would have that prior to the one of the witnesses appearing here, which is a son of the person who gave this statement, theoretically, we would be in a situation to challenge his credibility, maybe to challenge another line of evidence of the Prosecution. And also, allow me to say, despite of all my efforts in, I would say, [indiscernible] with the Prosecution, on many occasions I kindly ask my colleague, Mr. Di Fazio, to provide me with the exact dates when he made these so-called proofing notes in connection with his interview with Mr. Todorovic who is now in Spain. Up to now, I don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's deal with this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So this particular document, Your Honour, I would say is the only peak of the iceberg of the problem that we are facing here with this behaviour and action of the Prosecution. This document is just an illustration, and I made these so many references on the other documents. And God knows, Your Honours, how many documents we shall have during our proceedings on this manner, and I think that according to your ruling, this should stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. No. No. Can you wind up. You have had this document since yesterday. I'm sure you've got instructions. You discussed with your colleagues. Is there any point on prejudice and possible remedies that you would like to make submissions on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is always a possibility for remedies, Your Honour. We have an appeal proceedings. We have a possibility to call again one of these witnesses in question, which will bring us to another delay. And I think in general, it is absolutely a lack of diligence from the side of the Prosecution, especially after the ruling that this Trial Chamber made on the 19th of February. So I don't know what else as a Defence we have to do or wait for another action from -- ambush or something with regard to the evidence and statements, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is nothing you can do. You can only deal with the matter which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can only deal with the matter which is on record now. You can't focus on the future of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course. Let me give an answer in general terms, because I'm not able in capacity of Defence counsel to elaborate what I will do with a certain portion of statements or certain evidence in process of defence of my client because simply, that's Defence strategy, and I will see when and how I will act with that regard. In this particular case, as I said, we could call even the person in question of this particular statement, or we can call again one of the witnesses. But it also has certain impact of this process, of the delays of the fairness, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. No. No. You see it is open to the Defence to make submissions and ask for remedies from the Trial Chamber during the proceedings, at any stage during the proceedings. And the Trial Chamber will be able to make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. In conclusion, Your Honours, on the basis of all what I said, and on the basis of your ruling of February 19, I respectfully ask this Trial Chamber to take necessary actions against this practice of the Prosecution which is, I would say, with a constant and pertinent matter. That's my submission, Your Honours, with regard to this intolerable practice of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What sanctions are available?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to the Rule -- according to the Rule 68 bis, it depends on each Trial Chamber. Possible sanction could be that this case will be dismissed because of the lack of diligence of the Prosecution. Possible sanction could be to some extent -- I think there are elements that this behaviour is very close to the Rule 77 and contempt of the Tribunal, because we have numerous problems. This is a violation of the speediness of trial, fairness of trial. Also, there are certain impacts on the budget of this Tribunal because the witnesses should come again here. We are wasting our precious time, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. Let me be clear about that. There is already an Appeals Chamber decision that the judicial economy is not going to surpass the interest of justice. So don't worry about judicial economy. We are dealing with a criminal trial here. What should interest you is the fairness of the trial. What options are open to the Defence to remedy whatever prejudice they may submit that they have suffered?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that we have to discuss that matter with my colleagues, because at this moment, beside the things that I just mentioned, I would respectfully leave to this Honourable Trial Chamber to decide how this practice will be prevented in future. And also, if my learned friends and colleagues from the Defence teams would like to add something, I don't know if it is appropriate maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you are through. You are finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am finished, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel who wishes to make any submission on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours, I would just like to add a couple of points. First of all, I would like to clarify one thing with the -- with this witness statement. In the witness statement, it is clearly stated that the witness has said: "But my sons were with a group of men who offered resistance through the first day. Both of my sons had weapons." So there was an actual reference to how many children this person has. I'm not saying that our colleagues from the Prosecutors' side did anything in bad faith. We are not saying this. But Your Honours, out of the -- my main concern is the principle of fairness in this trial. We are -- it is in my mind it is very clear that the equality of arms before this trial -- before this Tribunal has always been an issue, and we as a Defence have always raised this issue that we are on the lower side of this equality of arms. What is our position is that at least, as a minimum, we should expect our learned colleagues from the Prosecutors' side to disclose all possible documents and witness statements which are connected to this -- to a certain particular case where we can find out whether, or they have the obligation under the Rule 68 as well. But I understand that sometimes it's very hard to determine because of the lack of the knowledge of the language and all that. I understand that is the problem for the Prosecutor, that these things might happen, can happen, and it's obvious they are happening. But then, why we were not disclosed all the witness statements pertaining to this case so we can find out. We had the time enough for that. In this particular witness statement, we have heard the witness over here, Mr. Esad Dagovic. Twice he was summoned, he gave his statement -- testimony in chief, and then was summoned for the cross-examination. The main point the Defence was making is that he was participating on the 17th of April in the fight with weapons, that he was fighting the other party on that particular date. He, himself, stated that it is not true. And we -- of course it creates a lot of prejudice for us. Because if we knew before that his father actually is confirming what the Defence has anticipated has happened or had some indications has happened, we would have done so many other things in this respect to find out and challenge the credibility of this witness, as we are authorised to according to Rule 68. The other thing, Your Honour, is that in this particular situation, just as a principle of fairness, in this particular case, we are now, you know, on I believe the 18th witness. Out of the 18, we already have 25 per cent, one quarter, three or four witnesses, who have to come back. First of all, there is Donia, then -- Mr. Donia, then Ibrahim Salkic. The same thing. We received one statement from one of the witness's of the Prosecutor only after we finished the cross-examination of Ibrahim Salkic. We raise this issue, and we wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'd just like to clarify from Mr. Zecevic. I think the implications that this is happened on two other occasions and these people are being recalled for the same reason. If they want to recall Mr. Donia that's because of a confidential document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, can you slow down. The interpreters have to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My sincere apologies to the interpreter. I'd like just to stop Mr. Zecevic just on this specific line of submission he is making because he is clearly trying to imply that our behaviour has resulted in the recall of two other witnesses he has named. That is simply not true. If the Defence want to recall Mr. Donia, they can do so and they can do so because -- they can request they can do so because there was a report here from another case which was confidential, which he submitted in front of another Chamber and the Defence did not take the steps early enough to have that -- the Prosecution did not oppose the lifting of the confidentiality of that. We couldn't give it to them without the Trial Chamber saying so. It is not even clear if that report is any way useful to the Defence anyhow. The seconds one, Mr. Salkic, I'm not even clear what Mr. Zecevic is referring to. If they want to recall Mr. Salkic because they have other questions to put to him as part of their Defence, that's their Defence case. But it's not a similar situation to the one that we are facing now with all due respect. And I object to Mr. Zecevic trying to say that this is the third time that we have arrived at a similar situation because it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would very much appreciate if I would be given the opportunity to finish, and then have the comments from my learned colleagues, because it was not my intention to imply that. I'm just -- my intention is to combine the principle of fairness, which among other things, guarantees to the accused, our clients, that they will have a speedy trial and a fair trial. The problem is this: We right now are in a position that we have the opportunity to recall Mr. Robert Donia, and that is very true what Ms. Reidy said, based on the confidential document which was not disclosed to us, and we asked for the permission for that. But the other thing was that Ibrahim Salkic, Ibrahim Salkic himself was here, he was cross-examined, only after the finish of his cross-examination, we received one statement which is clearly contradicting his statement -- his testimony over here. Now we have this statement by the father of Mr. Esad Dagovic which clearly contradicts the testimony of the witness which we brought over here. So what I am saying is I am not implying that the -- that my friends from the Prosecutor side did that on purpose. I'm just stating that this goes into the principle -- into the principle of fairness of this trial, and the length of this trial, that if we are in a position -- what I am trying to say is that it does not only affect the Defence case; it affects the case altogether. Because if we are -- we are entitled, I assume, to ask the permission by this Trial Chamber that we bring back Mr. Esad Dagovic and Mr. Ibrahim Salkic for recross-examination based on these two statements which we received after their cross-examination. I believe we are entitled to that. But who can guarantee that there isn't many more like this, and then we are going to be in a position where we could have at the very end of the Prosecutor case another recalling of let's say ten witnesses, which will undoubtedly prolong the case which we are hearing right now. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic? You also want to make a submission on this very document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One matter related to precision, and another thing has to do with a fact raised by my colleagues. Yesterday to the question posed by Judge Lindholm whether anyone is opposed to this statement, "he basically has nothing to say about the defenders." Today, Ms. Reidy corrected herself saying that the statement after all does mention one of the accused, and that the witness actually refers to Mr. Tadic. Let me make this clear: The Prosecutor made this reference sound less important than it was, saying that he was just "... I did not pay to be exchanged. I just went to one of his clerks and registered it myself -- to be about eight months. Saying that he was just in charge of his exchange, and that was just for purposes of clarification. Another matter I wanted to raise is the same as my colleague Mr. Zecevic and my colleague Mr. Pantelic have raised. It is not the issue here whether the Defence will be allowed to recall this witness. I believe the Trial Chamber would give us that permission anyway. But there is another problem which has to do with the so-called line of cross-examination. It is not the same thing to recall a witness for recross as our Trial Chamber itself has pointed out, saying that the cross-examination is an art. The Defence has to have complete information in order to build its strategy of cross-examination. As an example, when I cross-examined Witness M, I had occasion to experience this because of late disclosure. I presented to this witness his own statement given to the SUP and asked him about his signature. The witness had said that he always signed himself with his full name and surname. After cross-examination by one of my colleagues, the Prosecution team gave us another statement made by this witness given to Defence organs in Donji Levac, and the witness replied something entirely different. I believe that if I had asked, I would have been allowed to recross. However, it was my colleagues Zecevic who conducted the cross-examination. However, I want to say just that if I had had this document before my cross, I would have examined him differently. If at the moment of my cross-examination I do not have this document, and I am given it later, then the very purpose and outcome of my cross-examination is jeopardised. When you asked my colleague Mr. Pantelic about possible sanctions, I had two ideas: One possible solution is not to take the testimony of such a witness into consideration at all; and another possibility is to allow the Defence additional days to verify through their investigators the allegations made. I think the Trial Chamber would be fair to allow that because the Trial Chamber should, I think, also take into account among other things the amount of time given to each side to prepare and verify their evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be brief. I share the concern expressed by all of my colleagues, and I believe the Trial Chamber as well. And I believe that after all this, our concern will also be shared by our learned friends from the Prosecution. We do have to invest every effort to ensure that this trial meet the highest standards of justice because that is a task we all share, and we have to persist in these efforts. The facts quoted by my colleagues, and they are true, have indeed brought us to the present situation from which we now have to find a way out, a way out which would be useful and just for all of us involved in the proceedings. And first and foremost be fair to the accused and protect their rights. We cannot say by any means that our Defence will not be prejudiced by the omissions made, because any information, and especially information coming from the Prosecution, is very important for the preparation of our Defence and cross-examination. If the Trial Chamber recalls, and they surely do, Witness Esad Dagovic came close to assuming the role of Prosecutor in this courtroom. And it is certain that had we had this statement earlier, we would have charted our cross-examination quite differently and prevented him from behaving that way. I believe the Trial Chamber should take steps to prevent this from happening again. With all due respect for our learned friends from the Prosecution, and appreciation of their difficulties, I must say that although we are aware that they had predecessors in their current jobs, I would still have to ask them to make every effort to disclose to us all that they have, everything that they have. And I think that the Trial Chamber has already made a ruling ordering them to do so. As for possible solutions, maybe the ideas that have already been voiced here can be used for ensure that we, indeed, meet the principles of a fair and just trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will have the statement admitted for the limited purposes of making a ruling in this particular case. I wonder whether the Prosecution has extra copies for the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have five copies. Do we? Your Honour, I think perhaps we could provide at least three now to the senior legal officer, and then provide a number of other copies during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: There are four copies. There should be one for each of the members of the Bench and one for the senior legal officer, and we'll get another copy for the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And it will be admitted as a Court document.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's in English, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It's in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will discuss and give its ruling at a later stage during the proceedings. We can now proceed with the witness. I think he was still being cross-examined, if he can come into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You can continue with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Hadzijusufovic.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to complete as soon as I can. I promised the Trial Chamber I will take another hour, and we have already taken a lot of time to deal with other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the leave of the Trial Chamber, I would like to move into private session for three or four questions because I will be referring to protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said on page 52/1, on the 15th, that is just the unofficial transcript, because I got the official one only earlier today, on the 15th of April, you said that Miroslav Tadic put Catholics into the secondary school building, and later exchanged them. You said they were the first to be exchanged. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When Honourable Judge Williams asked you to clarify these facts, you responded to a repeated question of the Prosecutor saying that you had concluded so on the basis of the fact that that was the first camp to be closed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that you know or knew this based on what those people involved in the exchange had told you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was this camp closed, the camp in the secondary school building?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know, it was the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You hadn't been exchanged by that time, had you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that it was closed before the 30th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that only a few Croats remained in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand one thing. Perhaps you can explain. How Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. come the Croats that had been exchanged told you about this if they had been exchanged before you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats told me. I didn't say they had been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you then explain who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were coming from Dubica to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after the closure of this secondary school centre, there were no more Croats in Samac, that is, only a few remained. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you a couple of questions relating to this piece of paper, you described as having seen it on Tadic's desk. I will remind you of your own words. Dzevad Celic showed you a piece of paper that you had previously seen on Tadic's desk. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not previously. I saw the same kind -- type of paper on his desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you first saw this paper in Dzevad Celic's hands, and then you saw it on Tadic's desk?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not the same paper, but the same type of paper, the same form, the same format.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now speaking about Dzevad Celic. As you explained on page 7625 of the unofficial transcript of the 15th of April, he showed you a piece of paper containing the decision saying that you were to go to work, to the separation company.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that piece of paper, were there any other names, names of people who were supposed to go to the same place to work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that piece of paper contained only your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the text handwritten or typed? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it bear a stamp or signature?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How about signature?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look closely enough to see there was a signature, but it didn't bear a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said before this Trial Chamber, page 7910, also of the 15th of April, that you had seen a piece of paper on Tadic's desk, and you stated that you could not read the contents of the paper, the document; you only saw that it was the same form or format?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you couldn't read it? You couldn't see the contents?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be precise. Did you see your name on that paper on Tadic's desk?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Reading your unofficial, unsigned statement dated 1st of May, 1998, I noticed that you had stated the following: "On Tadic's desk --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think, and I'm not certain at this time, he is going to impeach him with a statement with a comment -- I don't know how you want to refer to it -- from not a statement as described under our rules, but an unsigned document which was never shown to him, which was never reviewed by him. And if that's what he is going to try and do -- if he is going to refresh his recollection, he could possibly do that by showing it to him if this witness has a memory problem. But to impeach him by something that was never signed, never read to him, never reviewed by him, I think that's a violation of the evidentiary rules if that is what he is going to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention, Your Honours, was just to ask the witness if he remembered the sentence, one of the sentences from his statement to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't read the sentence yet. I just want to ask him if he ever uttered it in his interview with the investigators. I don't intend to ask anything else, but he did have this interview with the investigators. I just want to ask him if he really said something to the investigators or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I suppose you can go ahead along that line of examination. You can go ahead with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you told the investigators that on Tadic's desk you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's the problem. You ask -- you read out the question, do you remember ever having said that? But not stating that, you know, the witness did say, that's a problem. It's a question of language, how you phrase the question. Because the way you phrased the question, you are holding it against him as if he did make the statement. He may not have made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the investigators that you had found on Tadic's desk a written order authorising certain people to go and pick up certain items they wanted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In response to a question I put to you yesterday, you answered that a member of the OTP showed you a note of the interview, your interview with the investigators, just before you came here to testify, and you said that you stood behind this note.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not recorded in my statement which I made under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll now read out to you what you said under oath. I'll read it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean in his testimony or -- can we be clear where that statement was made. Is it part of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That is part of his statement made to the Prosecutor just before he came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think there's a problem here of -- for two reasons. Number one, whenever he questions the witness, he says in your previous statement. Is he talking about the 1998 statement? Is he talking about two other Prosecutor summaries that were made with this witness in the past few months? The other thing I think -- whenever he talks about previous testimony, I think we should use the words "previous words" because that's confusing the witness and me and just refer to which one of these sheets of paper he's talking about, the 1998 or the Prosecutor summaries from 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And also, Mr. Lukic, to bear in mind that the Prosecutor's notes are not a statement of the witness. All right. So clearly identify what it is that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. But I would like to reply to my learned friend from the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor's notes do not indicate a date of the interview or discussions. We received two such summaries, one is not dated, and the other is dated the 24th of March, 2002. I believe both summaries or notes were drafted on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is, do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. Mr. Weiner, you heard what Mr. Lukic said, that one of the Prosecutor's notes is not dated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The last one is dated March 24th, 2002, and this one is not dated. I'll get a date at the break, which is in a couple minutes, for him, so they can refer to this by date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So you can go ahead, Mr. Lukic, as long as you declare if it's the one without the date or the dated one, then you indicate the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the undated note marked by the Prosecutor, paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what you discussed with the Prosecutor just before this trial in March of this year?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that occasion when describing the piece of paper you had seen on Tadic's desk, you said that it was an order for certain people to work on specific locations?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the paper was of the same contents, the same shape, the same format, and it looked the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you stick to the statement you made in your previous testimony, that you could not see the contents of this paper?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many days you worked in the separation company?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how many days, but I worked there for a long time, until the company was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But approximately?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 25th of August onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you could please tell me roughly, 15, 30 days.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that date, the 25th of August, is engraved in your memory for a reason?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after those people had made their escape across the Sava River, and it was after that that I was sent to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could take our break now, although I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take our break and continue the proceedings at 16.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I understand the witness is on his way. He is coming. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Prior to the break, I asked a question concerning your work in the separation plant. And you also indicated the period of time you spent there working.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that it was approximately 30 days at that location.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you some names, whether these people from Samac, whether they worked at separation, and if you know them. Do you know Ramic Resad?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the surname. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do not insist. Nedzad Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see him working at the separation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know Zivorad Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zile? Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see him at the separation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the foreman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Cviko?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last two names, they are Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Nenadic Tomislav?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Kalec Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let us pass to another subject. You have received three times a military summons for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was a mobilisation summons for the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you didn't react and report to that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported twice, on two summonses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened when you reported?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went in front of the memorial home, and we were told three times, also the second time, whoever wants to, to join the army, to remain -- to sign up. And who doesn't want, to go out and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know any of the people who signed up for the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, nobody did, at least as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was leaving, but I heard that some people signed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, before you continue, I just want to be clear in my mind when you are talking about the army of Republika Srpska, is this the same as the [indiscernible] or different?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can ask the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question, the summonses you've received for mobilisation on three occasions, did they refer to the same unit?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The summonses were identical, were the same. One I had submitted, the one that I had with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will also ask you in connection with the summons you've submitted. Do you know that those who signed up for mobilisation and joined the unit, that they hadn't -- didn't have to report for work assignments any more?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that. I don't know who signed up. I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned that you were the JNA staff sergeant in reserve? After serving the army, you gained that rank. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that not to respond to a summons, according to the then law, was illegal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question is: "Do you know that not to respond to a summons according to then law was illegal?" There's an issue of what "then law" is. Is it the BiH law, the Yugoslavian law, the Republika Srpska law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have been through this similar line of questioning before, Mr. Lukic. If you can avoid it and rephrase your questions, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm ready and willing to answer that question. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object to any answer because that's a legal issue, and he is not a witness to offer a legal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You will not answer that question. Wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've described in your testimony on the 16th of April to the question of the Prosecution that these summonses for mobilisation were handed to you by Subasic Jusuf?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same person who also sent you notices for your work assignments?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Distinguished -- Your Honours, I would like to tender a document. It is the summons for mobilisation to the army of Republika Srpska which the witness has submitted to the Prosecution, and the Prosecution, on the basis of reciprocal disclosure to us. I would kindly ask the Registrar to hand it to all. I also have the official translation in English and the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I answer that question? Could I respond to that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know when this summons came. In 1988, I was relieved from military training of the Yugoslav army. They must have also had records and shouldn't have sent me these summonses at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Yes, counsel, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see this document in front of the witness. I would kindly ask that one copy be submitted to the witness and placed on the ELMO. If need be, I have additional copies in the Serbo-Croatian/Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the usher can assist with that, giving it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, Mr. Hadzijusufovic --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the summons that you have handed over to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was a summons submitted to you by Subasic Jusuf, one of the summonses you've received?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see a date here, but tell us, when did you receive this summons and was it on the date which is stated here on the document?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This summons, I did not receive on that date. I really -- I received it on the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is the date concerning when you were to report to the memorial hall, or did you --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son was in Samac, and I went there earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that this is the second summons that you've received?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- we went once earlier, and this is the second date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you read to us under item 1, number 1, what is below the summons. Can you read it to us.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Failure to answer this summons shall be prosecuted pursuant to Article 79 of the law of military service and Article 214 of the Criminal Code."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a stamp here, which is quite legible. Could you read for us what it says.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you responded to the summonses, did you take your medical results and also the decree by which you were relieved of all your duties?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I handed that in to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did that in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, the socialist republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you didn't have this documentation with you any more?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've stated that you were also sentenced to one year of imprisonment by the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from my brother-in-law when I had been exchanged. I heard that after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you didn't serve any sentence prior to your exchange?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you've stated yesterday, you made certain statements to the authorities in connection with your attempt to swim across the River Sava?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have also stated that during the exchange, you were put on a bus with military prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were from Batkovic, Samac, who were imprisoned in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you a few questions concerning the exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Lukic, you just wanted to refer it so that it can be numbered for identification only?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would ask that both versions, both the English and the B/C/S, be entered as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Can we have the numbers, please, as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The B/C/S version is Exhibit Number D34/3 ter, and the English translation is D34/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In connection with your exchange, could you explain to the Trial Chamber the process of this exchange. You mentioned yesterday that they brought you in buses to the point of exchange. I understood you that you went to a tent and you had to sign something. If you remember, if you recollect, please describe it in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tent was a UN tent, United Nations tent, plus UN vehicles. And we were lined up on one side; on the other side, the people were also lined up for the exchange towards Serbia. So it was one from our side who entered, then another from the other side entered. They call your name, they find your name. There was a table -- a desk inside the tent. It was a rather biggish tent. One could see into it, and it was open on both sides. It was a nice tent. You enter it. They find your name on the list. You sign. And you exit on the other side. The question was whether you are being exchanged and crossing over to Croatia of my own free will, I answered "yes," and they said: "Please go ahead."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you're going to ask, I apologise, but just in case, could you make sure that we find out from the witness who the persons were who called the names and so on and so forth in the UN tent. There's an assumption to be made here, but for the record, it would be good to have it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, that was to be my next question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the person who asked you whether you wished to cross over?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. That was the UNPROFOR, a Russian team. But I didn't know this person who asked us. The person asked in our language: "Do you wish to cross over on the other side?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next question, at that point in time in the tent, were only you and UNPROFOR representatives attending there? Were they the only ones?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time you were signing, was Miroslav Tadic also present?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was outside with our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the representatives of the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also standing outside the tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So when that question was being asked to you in the tent, there were only the international representatives?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and people who spoke our language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how distant was the bus from the tent?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 100 -- I really do not recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you entered this tent in groups of eight?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We entered the tent one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from the bus to the tent, did you go in groups? If you cannot recollect, I will not insist.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET HADZIJUSUFOVIC [Resumed]
